title: The Stale Gate: Pricing and Diagnosing Drift in Judge-Gated AI Systems
content: Judge scores increasingly control downstream actions in AI systems, yet a threshold calibrated at one operatingpoint can retain authority after the judge or workload changes. The threshold remains fixed while its relationship tocorrectness, cost, and accepted-cohort performance can drift. Here, we introduce the stale gate, a versioned operationalcontract that links score-based routing to an explicit decision cost and two monitored promises: accepted outcomesshould remain consistent with the judge’s stated probabilities, and the accepted cohort should retain a declared referenceperformance. For calibrated scores, we derive the cost-minimizing threshold and use predeclared restart banks ofanytime-valid e-processes to test whether either contract has expired. In controlled experiments, we show that additiveoverconfidence of 0.15 increased accepted failure from 0.241 to 0.320 and expected cost by 0.327 per task. We findthat the restart bank alarmed in 16 of 5,000 no-drift deployments, tracked first-order delay within 1–4% over fiveshifts, and reduced mean epoch-8 detection delay from 585 to 156 audited labels. Across 80 prospective API-serveddeployments, we observe that the same judge edit produced a 0.424 claim gap with onset-epoch alarms in 5/5 GSM8Kdeployments but a 0.068 gap with no transition in 10/10 MBPP deployments; an honestly reported harder arithmeticworkload changed routing without triggering a claim-contract alarm. These findings show that score authority shouldbe treated as versioned evidence: drift can be priced, failed contracts distinguished, and gates recalibrated when theevidence supporting their decisions no longer applies. Together, these results provide a basis for managing the validityof judge-gated decisions over time, while studies across broader models and long-horizon settings can determine howthese controls generalize to evolving AI systems.
